title: Don't ruin my world (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 7:13)
hookLine: God shows Adam the trees: all this is for you; don't spoil My world
tomorrow: which verse holds the whole Torah? two rabbis split.

lines: LEAVE IT HOW YOU FOUND IT.
cards: Somebody hands you the keys to a place: a borrowed car, a friend's apartment for the weekend, a dorm room someone else lived in first. There's always one sentence on the way out the door. Leave it the way you found it.
The rabbis imagined God saying a version of that sentence to the first human, in the garden, right after handing him the keys.

teach.b: It's in Ecclesiastes Rabbah, on a verse that sounds tired: "Consider the work of God; for who can make that straight, which He hath made crooked?"

When the Holy One created the first human, the midrash says, He took him around all the trees of the garden of Eden and said: see My works, how beautiful and fine they are. Everything I created, I created for you.
Take care not to spoil or destroy My world, because if you spoil it, there is no one to repair it after you. Two things live in that speech. The first is gift.
The midrash doesn't open with a warning.
It opens with a tour, the way you'd walk someone through a house you built for them: this is for you.

teach.h: NO ONE TO REPAIR IT AFTER.
teach.b: The second is weight. In the story there's no second gardener coming.

teach.h: TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.
teach.b: Genesis already gives the job, placing the man in the garden "to dress it and to keep it": work it, and guard it.
So in this reading, caring for the world isn't a hobby added later. It's there from the start, given in a garden with the trees standing right there. And it's personal.
Not the world. My world, and for you.

how: This midrash is often quoted in Jewish teaching about caring for the environment, including around Tu BiShvat, the new year of the trees, alongside the law of bal tashchit, not wasting or destroying.

games.q: what does “don't ruin my world” mean?
o: a rule that people may never cut down a tree
a curse spoken over the garden after the first sin
God's charge to guard a world given as a gift

games.q: the tour of the garden — tap the pairs.
p: God walks the first human past the trees
everything I created, I created for you
don't spoil or destroy My world
no one to repair it after you

s: caring for the earth is only a modern idea, not an old Jewish one
a midrash has God telling the first human: don't ruin My world.
the midrash starts with a warning
it starts with a tour: see how beautiful; it's all for you.
Genesis gives the first human the job of keeping the garden
to dress it and to keep it: work it and guard it.

games.q: your class is cleaning up a park and someone says: why bother, the city will just trash it again. what does the midrash answer?
o: true, it's the city's job; we're only guests in the world.
do it anyway: if it's spoiled, no one comes after to repair it.
only bother if the whole world agrees to clean up too.
games.why: in Ecclesiastes Rabbah the care is personal: My world, for you, and no one to repair it after you.

practice: Find one living thing you can see from where you are: a houseplant, a tree through the window, grass, even a weed in a crack. Look at it for the whole sit, as if someone had just walked you over and said: this is for you.
Notice one thing it needs that you could give it this week.

wordCard.voice: Don't ruin my world: God's words to the first human in Ecclesiastes Rabbah, after a tour of the trees. If it's spoiled, no one comes after to fix it.
